title: Requests, limits, QoS, and GPU requests

opening.headline: Explains why a pod is forcibly terminated due to memory insufficiency, in terms of how requests and limits affect scheduling and termination.
body: When the model server pod experiences increased load, it may suddenly be terminated, with the termination reason showing "OOMKilled". On the same node, some pods survive while others are evicted first. This difference originates from resource configurations.

In this class, we examine what requests and limits define individually, how the combination of these two values determines a QoS class, and how GPUs make requests. The goal is to distinguish the impact of these settings on scheduling and termination.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain requests, limits, and QoS classes
Resource configuration effects can be distinguished from scheduling and termination.

screens.title: The pod is forcibly terminated due to memory insufficiency
screens.lead: Three symptoms that appear when resource settings are incorrect. When you select each symptom, relevant considerations are displayed.

visual.alt: Scene showing memory usage rising above the limit line as the load increases, leading to the pod termination.

items.prompt: The model server pod is suddenly terminated when it experiences increased load.
items.answer: Normally functioning well, it only terminates when the load increases, which may result in high resource utilization exceeding a certain threshold. Model servers can experience significant memory usage when request volumes surge.

items.prompt: OOMKilled is logged as the termination reason
items.answer: OOMKilled means the container was terminated by the kernel because its memory usage exceeded the memory limit. This is not an error in the code, but a signal indicating that the actual memory usage surpassed the set limit.

items.prompt: Some pods survive, while others are evicted first.
items.answer: When node pressure occurs, kubelet determines eviction priority by considering whether resource requests are exceeded, pod priority, and the ratio of usage to requests. How requests and limits are specified affects this ordering.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: how do requests and limits function respectively in scheduling and termination?

screens.title: Preview: requests and limits
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: How do you set requests and limits?
items.answer: Initially, people often set values based on intuition or by directly copying examples. However, since the two values serve different purposes—one is a reserved allocation for placement and the other is an upper limit on usage—the roles must be understood before assigning reasonable values.

items.prompt: Do you have a criterion for treating them as equal values or as different values?
items.answer: If set the same, it becomes predictable and has a lower eviction priority; if set different, it allows fewer reservations under normal conditions but enables greater usage when needed. Which approach is better depends on the service's load patterns and importance.

items.prompt: Will memory and CPU reach the same limit?
items.answer: They are not the same. The CPU may lead to throttling that delays usage, but memory may result in container termination. Therefore, even with the same limit settings, the risk levels for CPU and memory differ.

screens.outro: Let's first check the difference in role between the two values.

screens.title: requests are reservations, limits are caps
screens.lead: Select the button to change the state and alternatively compare how requests and limits each play a role.

visual.alt: Requests illustrate the scheduling priority criteria, while limits show the hard caps enforced by kubelet.

states.label: requests: reservation volume
states.body:
`requests` is a value used by the scheduler to determine on which node to place a pod. The scheduler places a pod on a node where the sum of the requests from already-scheduled pods on that node plus the request of the new pod does not exceed the node's capacity. Kubelet ensures that the container has at least the requested amount of resources reserved so it can use them.

Requests are not upper limits. If there is available capacity on the node, a container may use more than its requested amount. For example, even if the memory request is set to 256MiB, the container may use more if there is available capacity on the node.

states.label: limits: upper bound
states.body:
`limits` is a hard limit enforced by kubelet and the container runtime, and then by the kernel to prevent containers from exceeding resource usage. CPU limits are enforced through throttling; as usage approaches the limit, the kernel restricts CPU access. A container cannot use more CPU than its specified limit.

Memory limits are enforced through OOM (Out-of-Memory) termination. If a container uses more memory than its limit, the kernel may terminate it when it detects memory pressure. Therefore, memory limits are enforced post-facto, and while a container exceeding its limit may not be terminated immediately, it always remains at risk of termination.

screens.outro: Next, we examine the QoS class generated by the combination of these two values and the GPU request method.

screens.title: QoS Class and GPU Request
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the conditions of QoS classes and how to request GPU access.

visual.alt: Decision diagram that divides into three QoS classes based on combinations of requests and limits, with a defined eviction order.
labels: Do all containers have CPU and memory requests and limits, and are they the same?
Is there a request or a limit?
Eviction order when node resource is insufficient: BestEffort, Burstable, Guaranteed

tabs.label: Guaranteed
tabs.body:
In all Pod containers, both CPU and memory requests and limits are specified, and if the requests and limits are equal for each resource, the value is `Guaranteed`. The value must be greater than zero.

The Pod is least likely to be evicted when it has the strictest limits. It will not be terminated unless it exceeds its limit or until there are no lower-priority Pods to evict. Conversely, it is not permitted to use resources beyond its limit.

tabs.label: Burstable
tabs.body:
`Guaranteed` If no conditions are satisfied and any container within the pod has memory or CPU requests or limits, this is `Burstable`.

With requests, there is a minimum level of resource guarantee; if no limits are specified, resources can be flexibly used when node capacity exceeds the available limit. When node pressure occurs, both whether requests are exceeded and pod priority must be considered together, so the exit order cannot be determined solely by QoS class.

tabs.label: BestEffort
tabs.body: The pod `BestEffort` has neither CPU nor memory requests nor limits. While it can use remaining resources, since it has no requests, using resources may cause it to exceed its requested limits. Therefore, it is vulnerable to node pressure, and its actual eviction priority is determined by resource utilization and pod priority settings.

tabs.label: GPU Request
tabs.body:
GPU requests extended resources exposed by the device plugin. Once the plugin is installed, the cluster exposes schedulable resources such as `nvidia.com/gpu` or `amd.com/gpu`, and containers request these resources by name, similar to CPU or memory.

GPU is only specified for `limits`. If only limits are used, the request value will be filled with the same value as the limit; when both limits and requests are specified, the values must be identical; requests cannot be specified alone.

screens.outro: Now let's examine the case of a model server with low limits being terminated.

screens.title: Explanation: Shutdown of a model server with low limits
screens.lead: The instructor reads and modifies the resource settings of a model server that is terminated due to OOMKilled and then follows along by selecting the right arrow.

visual.alt: A screen displaying side by side both configurations with only a memory limit set and those with both request and limit defined.

steps.title: Step 1: Read the settings
steps.body: The `resources` model server container contains only `limits.memory: 2Gi`, with no `requests` or CPU allocation. Memory usage increases significantly when loading the model and further rises during request processing. The pod gets terminated by OOMKilled as load increases.

steps.title: Step 2: Examines how the request is populated
steps.body: If only a limit is specified and no request is provided, and if there is no separate mechanism to apply a default request, Kubernetes copies the limit value to use as the request. Therefore, this pod's memory request also becomes 2Gi, making both values equal. Since no CPU settings are specified, this pod is `Burstable`.

steps.title: Step 3: Usage exceeds the limit
steps.body: Memory usage exceeds 2Gi during model loading and request processing. The memory limit is enforced by the kernel resulting in an OOM (Out of Memory) termination, causing the container to exit with a status of `OOMKilled`. Even after restart, the same process repeats, leading to continuous recurrence during periods of increased load.

steps.title: Step 4: The cause is that the limit was lower than the actual usage.
steps.body: The cause is not a bug in the code, but rather that the limit is set lower than the actual maximum usage. Similarly, scheduling can mistakenly determine that a node can accommodate a pod because the requested resource is lower than the actual requirement, leading to the pod being scheduled on a node that is resource-constrained.

steps.title: Step 5: Adjust again based on model size and throughput.
steps.body: First, measure the actual memory usage both after model loading and under load conditions. Set `limits.memory` by adding headroom to the measured maximum, and set `requests.memory` by reflecting typical usage levels. Consider that increased memory usage occurs when both the model weight size and the number of concurrent requests increase.

steps.title: Step 6: If they are made equal, then Guaranteed becomes true.
steps.body: If both requests and limits for CPU and memory are specified and set to the same values, the pod becomes `Guaranteed`. When node resources are insufficient, the pod's eviction priority becomes the lowest, and memory usage is restricted to within the limit. If GPU is required, specify `limits` together with `nvidia.com/gpu`.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key takeaway: requests relate to scheduling, limits relate to ceilings.
screens.lead: This course content is summarized by the roles of two values, QoS class, and GPU requests.

paragraphs: **requests and limits**: requests are the reservation quantities that the scheduler uses to select nodes, while limits are hard upper bounds enforced on containers. CPU limits are enforced through throttling, and memory limits result in OOM (Out-of-Memory) termination.

**QoS Class**: The combination of request and limit defines `Guaranteed`, `Burstable`, and `BestEffort`. The actual node pressure eviction priority is determined jointly by whether the request exceeds the limit, the pod's priority, and relative resource utilization, and is not solely determined by the QoS order. If only the limit is specified, the request is set to the same value as the limit.

**GPU Request**: Specifies the extended resources exposed by the device plugin to `limits`. When evaluating the impact of configurations, consider the request at the scheduling stage and the limit at the execution stage separately.

checks.q: What correctly describes what happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit and memory limit respectively?
options: Both of them have the scheduler moving pods to other nodes to alleviate the issue.
The CPU is forcibly throttled during OOM termination, memory is throttled.
The CPU is throttled, and memory is forcibly terminated via OOM.

checks.explain: Limits are constraints enforced by kubelet. CPU is throttled to reduce usage, and memory is forcibly terminated via OOM (Out-of-Memory) kill if overuse is detected.

wrong.0: The scheduler sees a request and schedules it, but does not resolve limit violations by migrating the pod to another node.
wrong.1: The forced method has been reversed. Memory cannot be reduced and may result in termination.
wrong.3: limit is an upper bound that cannot be adjusted via request.

glossary.def: This is the reserved quota used for scheduling. Kubelet ensures that the container has at least this amount available.
A hard limit that forcibly prevents the container from overflowing.
Distinguished by Guaranteed, Burstable, and Best Effort, it influences the eviction order during node resource pressure.
This is a termination reason indicating that the kernel terminated the container due to memory limit exceeded.
This is a way of specifying the exposed extension resources (e.g., nvidia.com/gpu) in limits.

misconceptions.myth: limit is merely a reference value of the request.
misconceptions.fact: limit is the actual cap enforced by kubelet and the kernel. CPU is throttled, and memory leads to OOM termination.

misconceptions.myth: Using only limit means the request is 0.
misconceptions.fact: If no separate default request is specified, Kubernetes uses the limit value as the request.

misconceptions.myth: Exceeding the limits of CPU and memory results in the same outcome.
misconceptions.fact: The CPU may experience throttling with usage limitations, and memory may be affected by container termination.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: requests are for scheduling, limits are the upper bounds.
Memory limit exceeded can lead to OOM termination.
The combination of request and limit determines the QoS class.
